title: Primary 4 Tables, Line Graphs and Pie Charts
seo_title: P4 Tables, Line Graphs and Pie Charts Worksheets: Free Primary 4 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
short_title: Tables, line graphs and pie charts
standard_text: Completing a table from given data; reading and interpreting data from tables, line graphs and pie charts
meta_desc: Free P4 maths worksheets: complete tables, read line graph scales and trends, and read pie charts. 100 questions with answers, MOE syllabus.
key_big: Check the scale or the equal parts first, then read the value.
key_sub: A pie chart of 32 students has 8 equal parts, so each part is 32 ÷ 8 = 4 students, and 3 parts are 12 students.
body_html:
Tables: read across a row and down a column

A table puts data in rows and columns. Put one finger on the row and one on the column. The answer is where they meet. The Total row or column adds up the others.

FoodBoysGirlsTotal
Chicken rice8614
Prata5?12
Total131326
Example 1

Find the missing number of girls who chose prata.

Total − boys = girls: 12 − 5 = 7. Check the Girls column: 6 + 7 = 13.

Answer: 7 girls

Line graphs: check the scale first

A line graph shows how something changes. Before you read a point, ask: what is each gap between two gridlines worth? Go up from the bottom to the point, then across to the scale. A point halfway between two gridlines is halfway between their values.

Example 2

By how much did the number of visitors increase from Wednesday to Thursday?

Thursday: 70. Wednesday: 45. 70 − 45 = 25. This is the steepest part going up, so it is the greatest increase.

Answer: 25 visitors

Trends: a line going up shows an increase, a line going down shows a decrease, and a flat line shows no change. The steepest part shows the greatest change. The highest point is not always the greatest increase.

Pie charts: parts of a whole

A pie chart is a circle that stands for the whole group. Each slice is a fraction of the whole: half, a quarter or an eighth. Count the equal parts, then find that fraction of the total.

Example 3

How many students chose juice?

32 ÷ 8 = 4 students in each part. Juice has 3 parts: 3 × 4 = 12.

Answer: 12 students

Use a bar model when the question gives a difference. Milk is 4 units and juice is 3 units. If 4 more students chose milk than juice, then 1 unit = 4 students.

Comparing two pie charts

A bigger slice means a bigger fraction. It is only a bigger number if both pie charts show the same total. Half of 24 is 12, but 38 of 40 is 15.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting each gap on a line graph as 1Work out the scale: labels 0, 20, 40 with 2 gaps means 10 each
Reading the wrong row or column of a tablePut one finger on the row and one on the column
Taking the highest point as the greatest increaseLook for the steepest part of the line
Giving the number of parts instead of studentsDivide the total by the number of parts first
Saying a bigger slice always means more peopleWork out the numbers when the totals are different

faq.q: What is taught in P4 tables, line graphs and pie charts?
faq.a: In Primary 4, students complete tables from given data and read and interpret tables, line graphs and pie charts. They find totals and missing values, read scales, describe changes, and work out fractions of a whole from simple pie charts.

faq.q: How do I help my child read a line graph?
faq.a: Ask your child to find out what each gap between two gridlines is worth before reading any point. Then go up from the bottom axis to the point and across to the scale.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake with pie charts?
faq.a: The most common mistake is thinking a bigger slice always means more people. A slice only shows a fraction, so compare the numbers when two pie charts have different totals.

faq.q: Is this topic in the MOE syllabus?
faq.a: Yes. Tables, line graphs and pie charts are part of the Statistics strand in the MOE 2021 Primary 4 Mathematics syllabus. Students build on this in later years, up to the PSLE in Primary 6.

items.q: How many girls chose prata?
items.e: Go across the Prata row to the Girls column: 7. (5 is in the Boys column.)

items.q: How many students chose chicken rice altogether?
items.e: “Altogether” means boys and girls: 8 + 6 = 14. It is in the Total column.

items.q: How many students are there in 4E?
items.e: Look at the bottom right of the table: 19 boys + 20 girls = 39 students.

items.q: Which food did the fewest girls choose?
items.e: Read down the Girls column: 6, 7, 4, 3. The fewest is 3, nasi lemak. (Laksa has the fewest students in the Total column.)

items.q: How many more girls than boys chose prata?
items.e: Prata: 7 girls and 5 boys. “How many more” means subtract: 7 − 5 = 2.

items.q: What is the missing number of non-fiction books on Tuesday?
items.e: Total − fiction = non-fiction: 83 − 48 = 35. Rename 1 ten as 10 ones: 13 − 8 = 5, 7 − 4 = 3. (45 comes from 8 − 3 instead of renaming.)

items.q: What is the missing number of fiction books on Wednesday?
items.e: 92 − 37 = 55. Rename 1 ten as 10 ones: 12 − 7 = 5, 8 − 3 = 5. Check: 55 + 37 = 92. (65 comes from 7 − 2 instead of renaming.)

items.q: How many fiction books were borrowed on the three days altogether?
items.e: First find Wednesday: 92 − 37 = 55. Then add the Fiction column: 36 + 48 + 55 = 139.

items.q: How many students are in Chess?
items.e: Add the known rows: 28 + 35 + 19 = 82. Then total − 82: 106 − 82 = 24.

items.q: Which CCA has the most P4 students?
items.e: Compare the numbers: Choir 28, Football 35, Art Club 19, Chess 24. Football has the most.

items.q:
Mei Ling asked 12 friends for their favourite drink. These are the answers:
milk, juice, milk, water, soya milk, milk, juice, milk, water, milk, juice, milk
She puts the results in a table. What number goes in the Milk row?
items.e: Count “milk” one by one and tick each one: 6. Check the table: 6 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 12 friends.

items.q:
Mei Ling asked 12 friends for their favourite drink. These are the answers:
milk, juice, milk, water, soya milk, milk, juice, milk, water, milk, juice, milk
She puts the results in a table. What number goes in the Juice row?
items.e: Count “juice”: 3. Water has 2, soya milk has 1 and milk has 6. 6 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 12.

items.q: There are 36 students in 4A. 12 walk, 9 take the school bus and the rest come by car. What number goes in the Car row?
items.e: Walk and bus: 12 + 9 = 21. The rest: 36 − 21 = 15 come by car.

items.q: How many points did Blue House score in the relay?
items.e: 74 − 38 = 36. Rename 1 ten as 10 ones: 14 − 8 = 6, 6 − 3 = 3. (44 comes from 8 − 4 instead of renaming.)

items.q: Which house scored the most points altogether?
items.e: Use the Total column: Red 75, Blue 74, Green 81, Yellow 75. Green has the most.

items.q: Which house scored the most points in the races?
items.e: Green’s races: 81 − 42 = 39. Races column: Red 45, Blue 38, Green 39, Yellow 50. Yellow has the most. (Green has the most in the Total column, not the Races column.)

items.q: How many children went to the fun fair on Sunday?
items.e: 750 − 316 = 434. Rename 1 ten as 10 ones: 10 − 6 = 4, 4 − 1 = 3, 7 − 3 = 4. (446 comes from 6 − 0 instead of renaming.)

items.q: How many children went on the three days altogether?
items.e: Sunday: 750 − 316 = 434. Children column: 208 + 375 + 434 = 1017. (1698 adds the Total column.)

items.q: How many more children than adults went on Friday?
items.e: Friday: 208 children and 125 adults. 208 − 125 = 83. Rename 1 hundred as 10 tens. (123 comes from taking the smaller digit from the bigger one.)

items.q: How many mandarin oranges were sold on Thursday?
items.e: Monday to Wednesday: 240 + 185 + 310 = 735. Thursday: 1000 − 735 = 265. (375 comes from renaming each 0 as 10 without taking 1 from the next place. 1000 is 9 hundreds, 9 tens and 10 ones.)

sets.title: Read line graphs: scales and values

items.q: How many visitors were there on Monday?
items.e: Go up from Mon to the point, then across to the scale. The point is on the line for 40. (4 counts the gaps, but each gap is 10.)

items.q: The labels on the scale go up in 20s. How many visitors does each gap between two gridlines stand for?
items.e: There is one gridline between 0 and 20, so 20 is split into 2 gaps. 20 ÷ 2 = 10 visitors for each gap.

items.q: How many visitors were there on Tuesday?
items.e: The point for Tue is halfway between the gridlines for 50 and 60. Halfway between 50 and 60 is 55.

items.q: On which day were there 30 visitors?
items.e: Find 30 on the scale and go across to the line, then down: Wed. (Monday had 40.)

items.q: On which day were there the most visitors?
items.e: The highest point is above Thu: 70 visitors. Friday had 65, a little less.

items.q: What was the temperature at 10 am?
items.e: The scale starts at 24, not 0. Each gap is 1 °C. The point at 10 am is 1 gap above 28: 29 °C. (5 counts the gaps from the bottom but forgets that the scale starts at 24.)

items.q: What was the highest temperature?
items.e: The highest point is at 12 noon, on the line for 32: 32 °C. (34 is the top of the scale, not a reading.)

items.q: At what time was the temperature 30 °C?
items.e: Find 30 on the scale, go across to the line, then down: 11 am.

items.q: What was the temperature at 8 am?
items.e: The point at 8 am is on the line labelled 26: 26 °C. (24 is where the scale starts.)

items.q: How tall was the sunflower in week 3?
items.e: The labels go up in 20s, so each gap is 10 cm. Week 3 is halfway between 30 and 40: 35 cm.

items.q: In which week was the sunflower 55 cm tall?
items.e: 55 is halfway between 50 and 60. Go across to the line, then down: week 4.

items.q: How tall was the sunflower in week 6?
items.e: The point for week 6 is halfway between 80 and 90: 85 cm.

items.q: How many mandarin oranges were sold on Monday?
items.e: Each gap is 100 ÷ 2 = 50. The point for Mon is 1 gap above 100: 150 oranges. (3 counts the gaps, not their value.)

items.q: How many mandarin oranges were sold on Tuesday?
items.e: The point is halfway between the gridlines for 200 and 250. Halfway between 200 and 250 is 225.

items.q: On which day were 350 oranges sold?
items.e: 350 is the gridline halfway between 300 and 400. Go across to the line, then down: Thu.

items.q: How many oranges does each gap between two gridlines stand for?
items.e: The labels go up in 100s and there are 2 gaps between labels: 100 ÷ 2 = 50.

items.q: How much had Wei Ming saved by April?
items.e: Go up from Apr to the point, then across: it is on the line for 30. He had saved $30.

items.q: In which month did Wei Ming have $35?
items.e: Each gap is $5. $35 is halfway between 30 and 40. Go across to the line, then down: May.

items.q: How much water was in the pail after 6 minutes?
items.e: The labels go up in 4s and each gap is 2 ℓ. At 6 minutes the point is halfway between 8 and 10: 9 ℓ.

items.q: After how many minutes was there 15 ℓ of water in the pail?
items.e: 15 is halfway between 14 and 16. Go across to the line, then down: 10 minutes.

sets.title: Trends and changes in line graphs

items.q: How many more cups were sold on Thursday than on Monday?
items.e: Thursday: 70 cups. Monday: 40 cups. 70 − 40 = 30 cups.

items.q: Between which two days did the number of cups sold stay the same?
items.e: The line is flat from Tue to Wed: 50 cups on both days.

items.q: Between which two days did the number of cups sold go down?
items.e: The line goes down only from Thu (70) to Fri (60).

items.q: Between which two days was the greatest increase?
items.e: Look for the steepest part going up. Fri to Sat: 60 to 100, up 40 cups. Sunday has the highest point, but Sat to Sun is only up 10.

items.q: By how much did the sales increase from Friday to Saturday?
items.e: Saturday: 100. Friday: 60. 100 − 60 = 40 cups. (4 counts the gaps, but each gap is 10.)

items.q: How did the temperature change from 7 am to 1 pm?
items.e: From 7 am to 1 pm the line goes up all the time: 25, 27, 30, 32 °C. It increased.

items.q: By how much did the temperature fall from 1 pm to 7 pm?
items.e: 1 pm: 32 °C. 7 pm: 27 °C. 32 − 27 = 5 °C. (27 °C is the reading at 7 pm, not the fall.)

items.q: In which 2 hours did the temperature fall the most?
items.e: Falls: 1 pm to 3 pm: 1 °C; 3 pm to 5 pm: 3 °C; 5 pm to 7 pm: 1 °C. The steepest fall is 3 pm to 5 pm.

items.q: By how much did the temperature rise from 7 am to 1 pm?
items.e: 1 pm: 32 °C. 7 am: 25 °C. 32 − 25 = 7 °C. The scale starts at 24, so read the labels, not the gaps from the bottom.

items.q: In which week were both plants the same height?
items.e: The two lines meet at week 3: both plants were 9 cm tall.

items.q: How much taller was Plant B than Plant A in week 6?
items.e: Week 6: Plant B 18 cm, Plant A 16 cm. 18 − 16 = 2 cm.

items.q: Which plant grew more from week 1 to week 6?
items.e: Plant A: 16 − 4 = 12 cm. Plant B: 18 − 2 = 16 cm. Plant B grew more, even though it was shorter in week 1.

items.q: Which plant was taller in week 4?
items.e: Week 4: Plant A (solid line) 12 cm, Plant B (dashed line) 11 cm. Plant A was taller by 1 cm.

items.q: How did the amount of water in the tank change from Monday to Saturday?
items.e: The line goes down from 900 ℓ to 300 ℓ (it is flat for one day). Overall, it decreased.

items.q: Between which two days did the amount of water not change?
items.e: The line is flat from Wed to Thu: 650 ℓ on both days.

items.q: How much water was used from Monday to Saturday?
items.e: Monday: 900 ℓ. Saturday: 300 ℓ. 900 − 300 = 600 ℓ were used. (300 ℓ is what is left.)

items.q: Between which two days was the most water used?
items.e: The steepest fall is Thu to Fri: 650 − 400 = 250 ℓ. Saturday has the lowest point, but Fri to Sat is only 100 ℓ.

items.q: Between which two months did the number of books read go down?
items.e: The line goes down only from May (30) to Jun (22).

items.q: By how much did the number of books increase from January to May?
items.e: Each gap is 2 books. January: 12. May: 30. 30 − 12 = 18 books.

items.q: Which sentence describes the graph?
c: It fell every month until May, then rose
It rose every month until May, then fell
It stayed the same from January to May
It rose every month from January to June
items.e: 12, 16, 20, 26, 30: up every month until May. Then it fell to 22 in June.

sets.title: Read pie charts: halves, quarters and eighths

items.q: What fraction of the students chose mango?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Mango has 4 of them: 48 = 12 in simplest form.

items.q: Which fruit was chosen by a quarter of the students?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Watermelon has 2 of them: 28 = 14.

items.q: What fraction of the students chose durian?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Durian has 1 of them: 18.

items.q: What fraction of the students did not choose watermelon?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Watermelon has 2 of them, so 8 − 2 = 6 parts are not watermelon: 68 = 34 in simplest form.

items.q: What fraction of the students take the school bus?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. School bus has 3 of them: 38.

items.q: Which way of going to school is used by half of the students?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Walk has 4 of them: 48 = 12.

items.q: What fraction of the students take the school bus or come by car?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. School bus and Car have 4 of them: 48 = 12 in simplest form.

items.q: What fraction of the students chose Choir?
items.e: The circle is split into 4 equal parts. Choir has 2 of them: 24 = 12 in simplest form.

items.q: How many students chose mango?
items.e: Mango is half of the pie chart. Half of 40 = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 students. (4 is the number of parts, not students.)

items.q: How many students chose durian?
items.e: Durian is 1 of the 8 equal parts: 18 of 40 = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 students.

items.q: How many students chose watermelon?
items.e: Watermelon is 2 of the 8 parts = 14. 14 of 40 = 40 ÷ 4 = 10 students.

items.q: How many students take the school bus?
items.e: School bus is 38 of the pie chart. 24 ÷ 8 = 3 students in each part. 3 parts: 3 × 3 = 9 students.

items.q: How many students walk to school?
items.e: Walk is half of the pie chart. Half of 24 = 12 students.

items.q: How many more students walk than come by car?
items.e: Each part is 24 ÷ 8 = 3 students. Walk: 4 × 3 = 12. Car: 1 × 3 = 3. 12 − 3 = 9 students. (3 is the difference in parts, not students.)

items.q: How much did Ali spend on food?
items.e: Food is half of the pie chart. Half of $32 = $16.

items.q: How much did Ali spend on bus fare?
items.e: Bus fare is 2 of the 8 parts = 14. 14 of $32 = $32 ÷ 4 = $8.

items.q: 6 students chose Football. How many students were asked altogether?
items.e: Football is a quarter of the pie chart. If 14 is 6 students, the whole is 4 × 6 = 24 students. (12 doubles 6, but Football is a quarter, not a half.)

items.q: 3 students chose rambutan. How many students were asked altogether?
items.e: Rambutan is 18 of the pie chart. If 1 part is 3 students, 8 parts are 8 × 3 = 24 students.

items.q: Which two fruits together make a quarter of the pie chart?
items.e: A quarter of 8 parts is 2 parts. Durian (1 part) and rambutan (1 part) make 2 parts: 28 = 14.

items.q: How many students chose red?
items.e: Red is 58 of the pie chart. 16 ÷ 8 = 2 students in each part. 5 parts: 5 × 2 = 10 students. (5 is the number of parts.)

sets.title: Word problems with tables, line graphs and pie charts

items.q: Which class has more students who chose football?
items.e: 4A: 12 of 24 = 12 students. 4B: 38 of 40 = 40 ÷ 8 × 3 = 15 students. 4B has more, even though its football slice is smaller, because 4B has more students.

items.q: How many students chose football in 4A and 4B altogether?
Siti says, “More homes recycle in Block A, because its Recycle slice is bigger.” Is she right?
items.e: Block A: 12 of 80 = 40 homes. Block B: 38 of 120 = 120 ÷ 8 × 3 = 45 homes. The slice shows the fraction, not the number of homes.

items.q: Mrs Ng is completing a table of cans collected for recycling. 4A collected 3 times as many cans as 4C. Together they collected 168 cans. How many cans did 4A collect?
items.e: 4 units = 168, so 1 unit = 168 ÷ 4 = 42. 4A has 3 units: 3 × 42 = 126 cans. (56 uses 3 units instead of 4 units for the total.)

items.q: In a pie chart of favourite hawker food, chicken rice is 38 and prata is 18 of the circle. 12 more students chose chicken rice than prata. How many students were in the survey?
items.e: The circle has 8 units. Chicken rice is 3 units and prata is 1 unit. 2 units = 12, so 1 unit = 6. The whole survey is 8 units: 8 × 6 = 48 students.

items.q: Wei Ming wants to buy a watch that costs $65. He uses his savings in June. How much more money does he need?
items.e: June: $50. $65 − $50 = $15. (30 uses May’s savings, $35.)

items.q: The sunflower keeps growing by the same amount each week as from week 5 to week 6. How tall will it be in week 8?
items.e: Week 5: 70 cm. Week 6: 85 cm. It grows 15 cm a week. Week 7: 100 cm. Week 8: 115 cm.

items.q: How much money was collected from child tickets?
items.e: Child row: 60 tickets at $5 each. 60 × $5 = $300. (480 uses the adult price.)

items.q: How much money was collected altogether?
items.e: Adult: 45 × $8 = $360. Child: 60 × $5 = $300. $360 + $300 = $660. (105 is the number of tickets.)

items.q: Mrs Lim is making a table of the boys and girls in the Choir. There are 60 students in the Choir. There are 14 more girls than boys. How many boys are there?
items.e: Take away the extra 14 girls: 60 − 14 = 46. Now 2 units = 46, so 1 unit = 23. There are 23 boys (and 23 + 14 = 37 girls).

items.q: How much did Mrs Lim spend on food?
items.e: $2400 ÷ 8 = $300 for each part. Food has 3 parts: 3 × $300 = $900. (800 divides by 3, not 8.)

items.q: How much more did Mrs Lim spend on food than on transport?
items.e: Each part is $300. Food: $900. Transport: $300. $900 − $300 = $600. (1500 is the money not spent on food.)

items.q: Each cup of bubble tea costs $3. How much money did the stall collect on Saturday?
items.e: Saturday: 100 cups. 100 × $3 = $300. (330 uses Sunday’s 110 cups.)

items.q: After week 6, Plant B grows 3 cm every week. In which week will it be 27 cm tall?
items.e: Week 6: 18 cm. Week 7: 21 cm. Week 8: 24 cm. Week 9: 27 cm.

items.q: How many girls are there in 4A?
items.e: Girls in 4B and 4C: 19 + 20 = 39. 4A: 61 − 39 = 22 girls. (43 takes away 4A’s boys instead.)

items.q: Which class has the most students?
6 students chose Robotics. How many students chose Art?
items.e: Robotics is 1 of the 8 equal parts, so 1 part = 6 students. Art has 3 parts: 3 × 6 = 18 students. (48 is everyone in the survey.)

items.q: A bubble tea stall sold 3 times as many cups on Saturday as on Monday. It sold 60 more cups on Saturday than on Monday. How many cups did it sell on Monday?
items.e: Saturday has 2 more units than Monday. 2 units = 60, so 1 unit = 30 cups on Monday. (20 takes 60 as 3 units.)

items.q: Which graph is best to show how the height of a plant changes over 6 weeks?
items.e: The height changes over time. A line graph joins the readings so you can see it rise.

items.q: Pie charts for School A (400 students) and School B (600 students) both show a quarter of the students walking to school. How many more students walk in School B than in School A?
items.e: School A: 14 of 400 = 100. School B: 14 of 600 = 150. 150 − 100 = 50. The same slice does not mean the same number when the totals are different.
